CHIEF COMPLAINT
Big toe pain and redness for two weeks, worsening last week.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient reports throbbing pain in big toe with occasional sharp stabbing quality, especially with movement or prolonged walking. Symptoms began two weeks ago but significantly worsened last week during a trade show convention where patient could not walk the halls. Patient denies specific injury but notes redness and warmth to touch prompted concern. Pain worsens with light pressure, including contact with bed sheets at night. Patient reports walking on heel to avoid bending toe. Two ibuprofen daily has not provided relief. Symptoms worsen with downward movement of toe and improve somewhat with upward movement.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient reports toe pain worsened by bed sheets at night. Denies stomach problems. No other systems reviewed.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Not discussed.

MEDICATIONS
Ibuprofen 2 tablets daily.

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not discussed.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient is physically active, rides bikes regularly (over 800 miles in past year on trails), primarily wears flip-flops. Works on feet daily. Enjoys fishing and eating spicy Mexican food.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Inspection of foot and big toe. Range of motion testing of big toe joint: dorsiflexion present, plantarflexion limited to approximately 10-20 degrees with pain increasing at greater angles. Palpation reveals pain with medial-lateral motion of toe with grinding sensation, pain on lateral aspect of toe, and pain with palpation between first and second toes but less severe. Bone spur palpated on top of big toe joint.

RESULTS
X-ray of foot shows large spur on top of big toe joint and significant cartilage loss consistent with hallux rigidus (first metatarsophalangeal joint osteoarthritis).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Hallux rigidus with arthritis of first metatarsophalangeal joint. Start orthotic insert for shoe and meloxicam once daily for anti-inflammatory effect. Counseled on potential stomach irritation; patient to call if heartburn or substernal pain develops. Continue regular work and activities to evaluate treatment effectiveness. Follow-up appointment in two weeks. If no significant improvement, consider more invasive treatment options including intra-articular injection or surgical intervention (joint debridement or fusion) in future.
